```{r, include = F}
# load any other packages and read data here
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(knitr)
# get names
var_names <- read_csv('../data/biomarker-raw.csv', 
                     col_names = F, 
                     n_max = 2, 
                     col_select = -(1:2)) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(name = V1, 
         abbreviation = V2) %>%
  na.omit()

biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim <- read_csv('../data/biomarker-raw.csv', 
         skip = 2,
         col_select = -2L,
         col_names = c('group', 
                       'empty',
                       pull(var_names, abbreviation),
                       'ados'),
         na = c('-', '')) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  select(group, ados, everything())
```

## Abstract

This report examines how sensitive the protein biomarker analysis of 
Hewitson et al. (2021) is to choices made in its methodology. The data 
consist of serum levels of 1,317 proteins from 154 boys, 76 with autism 
spectrum disorder (ASD) and 78 typically developing (TD). We first explored 
the preprocessing. Raw protein levels are strongly right-skewed, which 
motivates the log transformation. Some subjects have many outlying values, 
but outliers are not concentrated in either group. We then modified the 
in-class selection pipeline, which combines t-tests and random forest 
importance and fits a logistic regression to the selected proteins. 
Selecting proteins on a training partition, rather than on the full dataset, 
lowered test AUROC from 0.883 to 0.789. This indicates the in-class results 
were inflated by data leakage. Selecting more proteins and combining the two 
methods' lists with a union instead of an intersection lowered performance 
further, to an AUROC of 0.742. Finally, we searched for alternative panels. 
A 3-protein panel (DERM, RELT, IgD), chosen by cross-validation, performed 
comparably to the 6-protein in-class panel (AUROC 0.766 vs. 0.789; accuracy 
0.688 vs. 0.656). A 24-protein LASSO panel offered no meaningful improvement 
(AUROC 0.797). Overall, a small, carefully selected panel does about as well 
as larger ones, though the small test sets limit how precisely the panels 
can be compared.

## Dataset

The biomarker data in this study comes from a selected sample of 154 youth males aged 18 months to 8 years. All subjects were screened to make sure that they did not have genetic, metabolic, physical, mental, or other neurological disorders. In the sample, 76 were classified as having autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and 78 were classified as typically developing (TD). The average age of the groups was 5.6 years and 5.7 years respectively. Within the ASD group, the 3 ethnicity classifications making up most of the sample are White (33/76), Hispanic/Latino (26/76) and Multiple Ethnicities/Other (9/76). Within the TD group, the 3 biggest ethnicity classifications were White (40/78), African American/Black (14/78) and Multiple Ethnicities/Other (14/78). Within both groups, a majority of subjects did not have any co-morbid conditions. The only co-morbid condition reported that affected a high number of people was seasonal allergies (30/76 in the ASD group and 17/78 in the TD group). All other co-morbid conditions affected no more than 2 people within each group. Lastly, a vast majority of subjects did not report taking psychiatric medications. All other psychiatric medications observed were taken by no more than 2 people.

The data was obtained by performing a fasting blood draw in the morning on the healthy subjects. The blood was then processed and analyzed through a Somascan™ assay to get information on the protein levels. The study obtained the levels of 1317 proteins from each of the 154 subjects, of which 192 proteins did not pass the study's quality control. For our work, all proteins were included. The data was preprocessed by applying a log10 transformation and then normalizing the data with a z-transformation. Furthermore, outliers with z-scores that were greater than 3 or less than -3 were clipped to 3 and -3 respectively.

## Summary of published analysis

The paper used 3 different methods to determine a panel of proteins for identifying ASD. The first method utilized a random forest that was trained 1000 times. Proteins were ranked based on their mean decrease in the Gini index, and the top 10 were selected for the random forest model. The second method utilized multiple t-tests. T-tests were conducted to identify the top 10 proteins with the most significant t-test values for identifying ASD. The last method utilized a correlation approach by calculating the correlation coefficient between protein levels and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) scores. The 10 proteins with the highest absolute value correlation coefficients were selected.

From the 3 methods, the paper found 5 proteins that were common across all testing methods. A logistic regression model was fit to these 5 proteins as a baseline for testing the predictive accuracy. Additional proteins that were identified from the other models were added one by one to see if they added any predictive power. The process was repeated 1000 times. Confounding factors were also tested by running t-tests and calculating Spearman's rank correlation.

The 5 core proteins that were flagged as significant in all 3 models were MAPK14, IgD, DERM, EPHB2 and suPAR. 4 additional proteins from the models were found to have increased the predictive power and AUC of the logistic regression model: ROR1, GI24, elF-4H, and ARSB. The AUC value for the model with these 9 proteins was 0.860±0.064. The sensitivity was 0.833±0.118 and the specificity was 0.846±0.118.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A(154 subjects) --> B(1317 protein measurements from subjects)
  B --> C(Random Forests for top 10 significant proteins) 
  B --> D(T-tests for top 10 significant proteins)
  B --> E(Correlation calculations for top 10 significant proteins)
  C & D & E --> F(Base logistic regression model with proteins in hard intersection)
  F --> G(Add other significant proteins 1 by 1 to the model if they increase accuracy)
  G --> H(9 proteins identified as the best panel)
```

## Findings

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

A couple of important choices were made in the data preprocessing. These were: (1) log-transforming the data, and (2) trimming outliers. These transformations were performed because the several of the distributions of protein levels had very large outliers which would have skewed the analysis. We investigated the distribution of protein levels for 5 proteins (PBEF, Carbonic anhydrase III, FGF-8B, TRAIL R1, and CNTN2) and observed a noticeable right skew in all of them. Below is a distribution of 1 of proteins observed.

```{r}
ggplot(data = biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim, aes(x = PBEF)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100) + 
  labs(x = "PBEF Level", y = "Frequency", title = "Distribution of PBEF Protein Levels")
```
Because of the skew of the raw protein levels, a log-transform would help transform the data to be more symmetric for the tests completed.

We also investigated the data before trimming outliers. Despite nearly every subject having some number of proteins with outlier levels (>3 standard deviations from the mean), only 8 have more than 80 outliers, while the rest have under 50.

```{r}
proteins_only <- biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim %>% select(-c(group, ados))
means <- colMeans(proteins_only , na.rm = TRUE)
sds   <- sapply(proteins_only , sd, na.rm = TRUE)

outliers_per_subject <- biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim  %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(outliers = sum(abs(c_across(names(proteins_only)) - means) > 3 * sds, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

barplot(outliers_per_subject %>% arrange(outliers %>% desc()) %>% pull(outliers), ylab = "Number of Outliers", xlab = "Subjects", main = "Number of Outlier Protein Levels per Subject")
```


Lastly, we looked at the number of outliers in each group. Since the number of outliers did not seem to significantly differ between the ASD and TD groups, trimming outliers should not bias the data in one direction too much.

```{r}
outliers_by_group <- outliers_per_subject %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  rename(Group = group) %>% 
  summarize("Average # of Outliers" = round(mean(outliers), 2), "Total # of Outliers" = sum(outliers))
outliers_by_group %>% kable()
```

### Methodological variations

```{r}
variations <- tribble(
  ~Analysis, ~`Train/test split`, ~Proteins, ~Sensitivity, ~Specificity, ~Accuracy, ~AUROC,
  "In-class (selection on full data)", "80/20", NA, 0.812, 0.733, 0.774, 0.883,
  "Selection on training set only", "80/20", 6, 0.688, 0.625, 0.656, 0.789,
  "Training only + top 15 + union", "75/25", NA, 0.579, 0.650, 0.615, 0.742
)
knitr::kable(variations, digits = 3,
             caption = "Test-set performance under each modification.")
```

**Selection on a training partition.** In the in-class analysis, the t-tests 
and random forest were run on the full dataset before the data was split. The 
test subjects therefore helped choose the proteins they were later used to 
evaluate. When we set aside 20% of the data first and ran every selection step 
on the training set only, the hard intersection gave a 6-protein panel (DERM, 
IgD, PTN, RELT, MAPK14, MAPK2). Test AUROC fell from 0.883 to 0.789, and 
accuracy fell from 0.774 to 0.656. This drop suggests the in-class results are 
optimistic because of data leakage. The training-only figures are a more honest 
estimate of how the panel would perform on new subjects.

**Larger panels and a fuzzy intersection.** We then took the top 15 proteins 
from each method instead of the top 10. We also replaced the hard intersection 
with a union, keeping any protein selected by *either* method, which gave a 
panel of 21 proteins. Selection was again done on a training partition (75/25, 
stratified by group). Performance dropped further: AUROC was 0.742, accuracy 
0.615, sensitivity 0.579 and specificity 0.650. These two changes were applied 
together, so we cannot fully separate their effects. Both, however, push in the 
same direction: they add lower-ranked proteins that carry weaker signal. With 
roughly 115 training subjects, a logistic regression on this many predictors 
likely overfits the training data rather than gaining predictive power. Being 
more selective, not less, appears to work better for this dataset.

These comparisons rely on a single test set each, of 31–39 subjects, so one 
misclassified subject shifts accuracy by about 0.03. The analyses also used 
different random splits. The direction of the changes is more reliable than 
their exact size.

### Improved classifier

```{r}
panels <- tribble(
  ~Panel, ~Proteins, ~Sensitivity, ~Specificity, ~Accuracy, ~AUROC,
  "In-class method (training only)", 6, 0.688, 0.625, 0.656, 0.789,
  "Simpler panel (DERM, RELT, IgD)", 3, 0.812, 0.562, 0.688, 0.766,
  "LASSO", 24, 0.688, 0.625, 0.656, 0.797
)
knitr::kable(panels, digits = 3,
             caption = "Alternative panels benchmarked against the in-class method on the same test set.")
```

We benchmarked two alternatives against the in-class method. All three panels 
were selected using only the training data and evaluated on the same held-out 
test set.

**Simpler panel.** We ranked the 6 baseline proteins by t-test p-value and fit 
logistic regressions using the top 1 through 6 proteins. To avoid using the 
test set to choose the panel size, we chose it by 5-fold cross-validation on 
the training data. We picked the smallest panel whose cross-validated AUROC was 
within 0.05 of the best. This gave a 3-protein panel: DERM, RELT and IgD. On 
the test set it reached an AUROC of 0.766 and accuracy of 0.688, compared with 
0.789 and 0.656 for the full 6-protein panel. Halving the panel therefore gives 
comparable performance, with slightly higher accuracy and sensitivity and 
slightly lower AUROC and specificity. A smaller panel would be cheaper to 
measure and easier to validate clinically.

**LASSO panel.** We also fit a LASSO logistic regression on all proteins, 
choosing the penalty by 10-fold cross-validation on the training data (λ.1se). 
LASSO selected 24 proteins, including 5 of the 6 baseline proteins (all except 
RELT). Its test AUROC was 0.797, and its sensitivity, specificity and accuracy 
matched the baseline. LASSO therefore did not meaningfully improve on the 
in-class panel and used four times as many proteins.

**Repeated splits.** Because a single test set of 32 subjects is noisy, we
repeated the whole procedure (train/test split, t-test and random forest
selection, simpler panel of size 3, and LASSO) over 20 random splits and
averaged the test set metrics.

```{r}
repeated <- tribble(
  ~Panel, ~Sensitivity, ~Specificity, ~Accuracy, ~AUROC, ~`AUROC SD`,
  "In-class method", 0.722, 0.719, 0.720, 0.780, 0.055,
  "Simpler panel (3 proteins)", 0.719, 0.706, 0.712, 0.773, 0.048,
  "LASSO", 0.706, 0.762, 0.734, 0.804, 0.059
)
knitr::kable(repeated, digits = 3,
             caption = "Average test set performance over 20 random splits.")
```

Across splits, the 3-protein panel stays within 0.01 AUROC of the in-class
panel, so the simpler panel holds up beyond the single split above. LASSO has
the highest average AUROC (0.804), but its gain of about 0.02 is smaller than
the split-to-split standard deviation (about 0.05) and it needs far more
proteins.

Overall, the simpler 3-protein panel is the most practical result: it performs
about as well as the in-class panel with half the proteins. DERM and IgD also
appear in the published core panel. LASSO may offer a small improvement, but
not one we can distinguish from variation between splits.
